anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model and indexing choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of plan selection quality.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or misleading statistics feed wrong cardinality estimates to the optimizer, causing sub-optimal plan choices even when the schema is adequate.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot ingest or apply primary redo fast enough, producing sustained replication lag and retention of transaction logs on the primary.

When all three root causes coincide, the database displays a blend of local performance pathologies and distributed-consistency issues. Queries on the primary show erratic and often escalating latency: some statements fall back to full scans because needed indexes are missing, while others pick inefficient join orders due to severe cardinality misestimates. These heavier plans inflate CPU, I/O, and lock footprints, lengthening transaction commit times. The enlarged transactions generate larger redo bursts, which replicas—already throughput-constrained—cannot replay promptly. Monitoring tools simultaneously report growing execution times, inflated actual-vs-estimated row count gaps, chronic automatic statistics refreshes that never catch up, and steadily widening replication delay with mounting log storage at both primary and replica sites. Stale read-only replicas deliver increasingly outdated data, and failovers risk data loss.

Causally, poor schema and index design magnifies the impact of bad statistics: missing or non-covering indexes force the optimizer to rely on table or index scans whose cost is underestimated when statistics are stale or skewed, leading to heavyweight execution plans. The resultant surge in I/O and longer-running transactions produce larger, more bursty WAL/redo streams. Replicas, already limited by apply inefficiencies or network constraints, fall behind faster as they must process the bloated redo generated by inefficient plans and possible full-table modifications (e.g., bulk updates without proper indexing). Conversely, replication lag can delay statistics refresh jobs that run on replicas or offload maintenance traffic, further extending statistics staleness on the primary. The intertwined feedback loop—design flaws causing heavier workload, statistics errors choosing worse plans, and replication lag preventing timely relief—drives systemic degradation across both transactional and analytical operations.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
